audience: Provisional ages 14–18; teacher adjusts reading and support
timingNote: 45 minutes is an authored planning estimate, not observed classroom timing.

definitions.draft: Authored teaching proposal; prepared sources may exist, but historical/source review and teacher approval are separate gates.
definitions.source_verified: Exact selected text, edition, locator, and provenance checked and saved; document attribution, context adequacy, and any applicable reuse notices must also be reviewed. Byte agreement alone is insufficient.
definitions.teacher_reviewed: Teacher approved objective, packet, reading boundary, accessibility, and content.
definitions.integrated: Pack loaded through trusted runtime contracts and exercised in a fresh classroom.
definitions.pilot_ready: Current build passed applicable PRODUCT-READINESS.md gates; separate from content status.

worlds.title: Alexandria: the systems that sustain knowledge
worlds.subject: history

source.title: Strabo, Geography 17.1.8
source.edition: H. L. Jones English translation (1932), LacusCurtius; exact saved Mouseion passage
source.verification: exact Mouseion passage saved with provenance and offsets; historical framing supplied separately; teacher review required

worlds.readingBoundary: 17.1.8 plus separately labeled local funding assumption and invented ledger
worlds.rationale: Existing setting makes this the first place to exercise the complete reasoning loop.
cautions: Strabo does not prove the proposed trade-to-funding mechanism.
The 12-to-4 ship ledger is invented.
No single-event destruction story or exact architectural reconstruction is established.
The Mouseion (Museum) described by Strabo is a scholarly institution; it is not interchangeable with a Library building or book collection.

lessons.title: Could knowledge survive a trade collapse?
lessons.inquiry: Under which assumptions would less trade reduce scholar support?
lessons.evidenceActivity: Classify source, assumption, and prop; draw a conditional chain with a citation at each supported step.
lessons.teacherChallenge: Which link does Strabo establish, and which link belongs only to this scenario?
lessons.revisionTask: Rewrite one inevitable outcome as a conditional claim and identify the missing evidence.

lessons.title: The replacement patron
lessons.inquiry: Could another source of support change the explanation?
lessons.sourceRange: Same approved packet; patron replacement is an explicit scenario assumption
lessons.evidenceActivity: Compare two funding diagrams while holding the disruption constant.
lessons.teacherChallenge: What would you need to observe to distinguish the two explanations?
lessons.revisionTask: Add a competing mechanism and one observation that could discriminate between them.

lessons.title: A building or a community?
lessons.inquiry: What can a description of an institution tell us about sustaining knowledge?
lessons.sourceRange: 17.1.8; existing card linked to original source
lessons.evidenceActivity: Separate statements about facilities, people, and institutional support from visual guesses.
lessons.teacherChallenge: Does a detailed building model add documentary evidence?
lessons.revisionTask: Refine the claim about preservation and state what this source cannot answer.

worlds.title: The Odyssey: cleverness, pride, and leadership
worlds.subject: literature
worlds.proposedScene: coast prototype; authored cave and ship later

source.title: Homer, The Odyssey
source.edition: Samuel Butler prose translation; use Ulysses in displayed excerpts
source.verification: selected excerpts and bounded context matched to pinned normalized source; teacher review required

worlds.readingBoundary: Book IX only; no later-book events, preface theories, or footnotes in model context
worlds.rationale: Explicit first literature priority in LITERATURE-EXPANSION.md.
cautions: Narrated choices are not a neutral historical record.
Mythic geography and staging are interpretations.
Violence stays in teacher-reviewed text; no combat reenactment.

lessons.title: The clever escape
lessons.inquiry: How does the account invite admiration for cleverness?
lessons.sourceRange: Book IX: cave encounter, assumed name, and escape
lessons.evidenceActivity: Annotate a decision and the narrator’s wording; distinguish action from self-presentation.
lessons.teacherChallenge: Is your evidence about what he does, or how he tells it?
lessons.revisionTask: Qualify the interpretation with one detail that complicates admiration.

lessons.title: The name shouted back
lessons.inquiry: How does revealing an identity change a reading of leadership?
lessons.sourceRange: Book IX: narrated stratagem evaluation, crew warning, and shouted identity
lessons.evidenceActivity: Compare the narrator’s claim of cleverness with his response to the crew’s warning; cite wording from both.
lessons.teacherChallenge: What does the crew’s objection make harder to explain?
lessons.revisionTask: Revise the leadership claim without reducing the episode to a single trait.

lessons.title: If the name stayed hidden
lessons.inquiry: What can a textual counterfactual reveal about the original choice?
lessons.sourceRange: Book IX: same departure packet only
lessons.evidenceActivity: Write a two-column comparison of textual evidence and invented consequences.
lessons.teacherChallenge: Which consequences are supported possibilities, and which are inventions?
lessons.revisionTask: Return to the original text and explain how the comparison changes your reading.

worlds.title: Pride and Prejudice: revising a judgment
worlds.subject: literature
worlds.proposedScene: garden prototype; authored Hunsford kit later

source.title: Jane Austen, Pride and Prejudice
source.edition: Project Gutenberg #1342; preserve selected edition and chapter numbering
source.verification: selected excerpts and bounded context matched to pinned normalized source; teacher review required

worlds.readingBoundary: Chapters 35–36 only; earlier material requires a separate teacher-approved packet; nothing after 36
worlds.rationale: Explicit second literature priority; makes evidence-based revision the lesson’s subject.
cautions: Darcy’s assertions are not independent corroboration.
Elizabeth’s reassessment is arguable, not a required answer.
Hunsford is not Pemberley; the room and desk are teaching staging.

lessons.title: A letter is a claim
lessons.inquiry: How should a reader evaluate a persuasive private letter?
lessons.evidenceActivity: Tag assertions, offered support, and appeals to the recipient.
lessons.teacherChallenge: What could this writer have an interest in emphasizing?
lessons.revisionTask: Replace automatic acceptance or rejection with a passage-supported assessment.

lessons.title: Reading again
lessons.inquiry: How does the narration represent Elizabeth’s reconsideration?
lessons.sourceRange: Chapter 36: first reading, rereading, and self-assessment; no direct Chapter 35 letter passage in this packet
lessons.evidenceActivity: Compare the narration of Elizabeth’s first reading, rereading, and self-assessment; distinguish her changing interpretation from independent proof.
lessons.teacherChallenge: Which phrase supports your account of the change, rather than just naming it?
lessons.revisionTask: Explain a change in interpretation through wording and acknowledge an alternative reading.

lessons.title: How far should judgment change?
lessons.inquiry: What remains uncertain after rereading?
lessons.evidenceActivity: Build a claim/support/remaining-question table using only assigned passages.
lessons.teacherChallenge: Which conclusion goes beyond what this packet allows you to know?
lessons.revisionTask: Narrow one overconfident conclusion and identify evidence that could change it.

worlds.title: Macbeth: persuasion and responsibility
worlds.subject: literature
worlds.proposedScene: archive prototype; castle threshold kit proposed

source.title: William Shakespeare, Macbeth
source.edition: Project Gutenberg #1533; act/scene locators until edition-specific lines are checked
source.verification: selected excerpts and bounded context matched to pinned normalized source; teacher review required

worlds.readingBoundary: Act 1 scenes 3, 5, and 7; no later outcome in tutor context
worlds.rationale: A compact comparison of multiple speakers supports close reading and defensible disagreement.
cautions: Supernatural staging must not assert that destiny removes responsibility.
Planned violence is discussed through the text, not a game action.

lessons.title: Hearing a prophecy
lessons.inquiry: How does Macbeth interpret what he hears?
lessons.evidenceActivity: Separate the reported prediction from the listener’s inference.
lessons.teacherChallenge: Which words belong to the speakers, and which belong to his response?
lessons.revisionTask: Revise a fate claim to account for interpretive choice.

lessons.title: Pressure in language
lessons.inquiry: How does persuasion work through appeals to identity?
lessons.evidenceActivity: Compare two appeals and explain a specific rhetorical choice.
lessons.teacherChallenge: Does forceful language prove that persuasion succeeded?
lessons.revisionTask: Distinguish rhetorical strategy from an inferred effect.

lessons.title: Reasons at the threshold
lessons.inquiry: How does a soliloquy complicate responsibility?
lessons.evidenceActivity: Pair an expressed objection with the subsequent decision language.
lessons.teacherChallenge: Can your interpretation account for the strongest objection?
lessons.revisionTask: Defend a reading that addresses both agency and pressure.

worlds.title: Frankenstein: ambition and responsibility
worlds.subject: literature
worlds.proposedScene: archive prototype; workshop and writing room proposed

source.title: Mary Shelley, Frankenstein
source.edition: 1831 edition, Project Gutenberg #42324; do not mix 1818 chapter divisions
source.verification: selected excerpts and bounded context matched to pinned normalized source; teacher review required

worlds.readingBoundary: Selected Letters I–II and Chapters 4–5 in the 1831 edition; each lesson uses only its saved excerpts and bounded context
worlds.rationale: Pairs a framing voice with a narrated act, enabling analysis of ambition and selective explanation.
cautions: Do not import film machinery or later plot as evidence.
Prepared excerpts match saved text; activity coverage and teacher approval remain separate checks.

lessons.title: Ambition in a letter
lessons.inquiry: How does a writer make an ambition seem worthwhile?
lessons.evidenceActivity: Mark an aspiration and a qualification in the same speaker’s account.
lessons.teacherChallenge: Who is being persuaded by this account?
lessons.revisionTask: Reframe the claim to include audience and a complicating detail.

lessons.title: The work and the telling
lessons.inquiry: How does retrospective narration shape a reader’s judgment?
lessons.evidenceActivity: Distinguish described action from later evaluative language.
lessons.teacherChallenge: Are you attributing hindsight to the earlier moment?
lessons.revisionTask: Separate the narrator’s retrospective stance from the character’s reported understanding.

lessons.title: Responsibility at the threshold
lessons.inquiry: What obligations does the creation episode invite readers to consider?
lessons.sourceRange: Chapter 5: selected creation and response passages
lessons.evidenceActivity: Compare the creator’s recalled goal in Chapter 5 with his response after creation, then argue from wording.
lessons.teacherChallenge: What alternative reading could explain the same passage?
lessons.revisionTask: Address that reading without inventing later testimony.

worlds.title: A Christmas Carol: learning to see others
worlds.subject: literature
worlds.proposedScene: archive prototype; counting house and domestic stations proposed

source.title: Charles Dickens, A Christmas Carol
source.edition: Project Gutenberg #46; selected prose text, illustrations excluded from evidence packet
source.verification: selected excerpts and bounded context matched to pinned normalized source; teacher review required

worlds.readingBoundary: Staves 1–3; no Staves 4–5 in character or tutor context
worlds.rationale: Recurring language and contrasting settings offer a manageable secondary literature pack.
cautions: Visual poverty is not evidence of a universal Victorian experience.
No ending spoilers or compulsory personal disclosure.

lessons.title: Distance in description
lessons.inquiry: How does narration establish distance or sympathy?
lessons.evidenceActivity: Compare a descriptive choice with dialogue and explain their effects.
lessons.teacherChallenge: Would the dialogue alone support the same reading?
lessons.revisionTask: Make the narrator’s contribution explicit.

lessons.title: The use of memory
lessons.inquiry: How does a remembered scene challenge an earlier judgment?
lessons.evidenceActivity: Link a memory passage to an initial interpretation.
lessons.teacherChallenge: What specifically changes in your evidence, not just the atmosphere?
lessons.revisionTask: Revise using the contrast while retaining an unresolved question.

lessons.title: A change of viewpoint
lessons.inquiry: How does a domestic scene redirect the reader’s attention?
lessons.evidenceActivity: Compare focal details and whose perspective receives attention.
lessons.teacherChallenge: Does sympathy establish every claim you made about the character?
lessons.revisionTask: Narrow the interpretation and support it with two details.

worlds.title: The Tempest: who tells the island’s story?
worlds.subject: literature
worlds.proposedScene: coast prototype; three narrative stations proposed

source.title: William Shakespeare, The Tempest
source.edition: Project Gutenberg #1540; act/scene locators, no invented line numbering
source.verification: selected excerpts and bounded context matched to pinned normalized source; teacher review required

worlds.rationale: Reuses a coast concept while assessing voice and competing accounts rather than escape.
cautions: Power and coercion require contextual discussion; dialogue does not make a speaker authoritative.
Island scenery cannot settle competing claims of ownership.
The selected edition attributes a speech to Prospero that Folger attributes to Miranda; flag this editorial difference before comparing speakers.

lessons.title: Authority in a storm
lessons.inquiry: How does crisis alter the language of authority?
lessons.evidenceActivity: Compare commands from different speakers and the grounds they offer.
lessons.teacherChallenge: Who claims authority, and what makes it effective within this scene?
lessons.revisionTask: Distinguish claimed status from demonstrated control.

lessons.title: A story with a listener
lessons.inquiry: How does Prospero direct Miranda’s attention?
lessons.evidenceActivity: Annotate a prompt, interruption, or emphasis alongside the story it frames.
lessons.teacherChallenge: How might the telling shape what the listener accepts?
lessons.revisionTask: Explain narrative control through a specific language choice.

lessons.title: Competing claims
lessons.inquiry: How should a reader weigh incompatible accounts of the island?
lessons.sourceRange: 1.2: approved Prospero, Ariel, and Caliban exchanges
lessons.evidenceActivity: Make a speaker/claim/support table without choosing by character prestige.
lessons.teacherChallenge: What can the scene establish, and what remains contested?
lessons.revisionTask: Address a competing account and the limits of the available text.

worlds.title: Philadelphia: the case for independence
worlds.subject: history

source.title: Declaration of Independence transcription
source.edition: National Archives transcription of the adopted Declaration
source.verification: selected excerpts and bounded context matched to pinned normalized source; teacher review required

worlds.readingBoundary: Approved selections from principles, grievances, and conclusion; contextual claims need additional sources
worlds.rationale: Document structure provides three meaningful stations without inventing eyewitness testimony.
cautions: A grievance is an allegation in an advocacy document, not independently verified by its presence.
Universal language does not establish universal participation or rights in practice.
Distinguish the independence vote (July 2, 1776), adoption (July 4), and most signatures on the engrossed copy (August 2).

lessons.title: Principles and conclusions
lessons.inquiry: How does the document connect its principles to political action?
lessons.evidenceActivity: Map a premise and conclusion to their exact textual support.
lessons.teacherChallenge: Does the passage state a principle or describe existing practice?
lessons.revisionTask: Separate the document’s argument from a claim about lived conditions.

lessons.title: What a grievance can prove
lessons.inquiry: How do accumulated grievances support persuasion?
lessons.evidenceActivity: Group allegations and identify the external evidence needed to test one.
lessons.teacherChallenge: Is repetition corroboration?
lessons.revisionTask: Qualify one historical claim by naming the source’s purpose and limits.

lessons.title: The declaration as an action
lessons.inquiry: What changes when an argument becomes a collective declaration?
lessons.evidenceActivity: Compare descriptive, justificatory, and declarative language.
lessons.teacherChallenge: Does announcing an outcome prove that it has been secured?
lessons.revisionTask: Distinguish an asserted political act from its unverified consequences.

worlds.title: Douglass: literacy, power, and testimony
worlds.subject: history
worlds.proposedScene: archive prototype; documentary reading room proposed

source.title: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
source.edition: 1845 Narrative, Project Gutenberg #23; retain author and autobiographical context
source.verification: selected excerpts and bounded context matched to pinned normalized source; teacher review required

worlds.readingBoundary: Chapters VI–VII; no invented escape scenes or later events
worlds.rationale: Extends source inquiry to authored testimony and the limits of historical generalization.
cautions: No slavery role-play, purchase mechanics, or simulated victim testimony.
Teacher previews discriminatory language and violence in the assigned text.
One narrative must not stand in for every enslaved person’s experience.
Auld’s claim that instruction was unlawful is reported speech, not proof of a Maryland statutory ban; distinguish household coercion from law.

lessons.title: Why restrict learning?
lessons.inquiry: How does the narrative connect control of literacy with power?
lessons.evidenceActivity: Separate reported speech, narrated experience, and the author’s interpretation.
lessons.teacherChallenge: Whose words support this claim, and who is reporting them?
lessons.revisionTask: Specify the chain of testimony and limit the generalization.

lessons.title: Learning under constraint
lessons.inquiry: What does the account show about agency within coercion?
lessons.evidenceActivity: Trace an action and its constraint with two textual references.
lessons.teacherChallenge: Does recognizing agency diminish the constraint described?
lessons.revisionTask: Account for both without presenting coercion as a game challenge.

lessons.title: Knowledge and its costs
lessons.inquiry: How does testimony complicate a simple story of progress?
lessons.sourceRange: Chapter VII: selected learning, argument, and distress passages
lessons.evidenceActivity: Compare an opportunity and a cost described by the narrator.
lessons.teacherChallenge: What does this account establish about this experience, and what needs corroboration?
lessons.revisionTask: Refine the explanation and identify a question for a second source.

worlds.title: Seneca Falls: rewriting a declaration
worlds.subject: history
worlds.proposedScene: archive prototype; declaration comparison room proposed

source.title: Declaration of Sentiments
source.edition: National Park Service transcription; pair with National Archives Declaration transcription
source.verification: selected excerpts and bounded context matched to pinned normalized source; teacher review required

worlds.readingBoundary: Selected Sentiments opening, grievances, and conclusion; approved 1776 parallel passages only
worlds.rationale: Reuses a documentary setting for comparison across sources and historical contexts.
cautions: Shared language does not mean identical circumstances.
Document signatories or authors do not represent all women’s experiences.
Text alone cannot establish policy implementation or movement outcomes.
The claim that all colleges excluded women needs qualification: Oberlin admitted women to its baccalaureate program in 1837.

lessons.title: Borrowing a public form
lessons.inquiry: How does adapting a familiar declaration strengthen a claim?
lessons.evidenceActivity: Align retained and altered wording and explain the significance.
lessons.teacherChallenge: Which inference comes from the wording, and which needs context?
lessons.revisionTask: Revise the comparison to acknowledge a difference in purpose or position.

lessons.title: Naming an injustice
lessons.inquiry: How do particular grievances support a general rights claim?
lessons.evidenceActivity: Connect one allegation to a principle and identify a corroborating-source need.
lessons.teacherChallenge: What additional record would help test the allegation historically?
lessons.revisionTask: Separate documentary assertion from independent confirmation.

lessons.title: From declaration to change
lessons.inquiry: What can a declaration tell us about a movement’s aims?
lessons.evidenceActivity: Distinguish stated aims, proposed action, and outcomes not in the packet.
lessons.teacherChallenge: What would be an unsupported claim of success?
lessons.revisionTask: State an evidence-bounded conclusion and a next research question.
